messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 27
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Animator
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 66

She is 27, a Latin American woman who works as an animator, and when she first begins to speak about what happened, she does so carefully, as if she is still trying to figure out which parts of her story are safe to say out loud. She describes the relationship as something that started with warmth and attention. Her partner seemed attentive in the beginning, proud of her work, interested in the worlds she created on screen, the characters she could bring to life frame by frame. She liked that he asked about her ideas and seemed to admire how she could stay up late sketching, coloring, and revising scenes until they moved the way she wanted. For a while, she thinks she has found someone who sees her.

The turning point, she says, comes gradually, then all at once. Small humiliations become sharp criticisms. Jealousy becomes control. He comments on where she goes, who she texts, why she is late, why she laughs at messages on her phone. She finds herself editing her words before speaking, scanning his face for changes in mood. The first time he grabs her arm hard enough to bruise, she tells herself it is a one-time thing, something he will regret. She does not yet call it abuse. She tells herself he is stressed, that everyone has bad moments, that love requires patience. Over time, the apologies become part of the cycle, and so do the threats, the shoving, the sudden bursts of rage that seem to come from nowhere. She learns to move around him in the apartment as if she is navigating a room full of glass.

The physical assaults increase in severity. She remembers the cold shock of being pinned against a wall, the air leaving her lungs when he strikes her, the way her body starts to anticipate danger before her mind fully names it. She begins to live in a state of constant alertness, listening for footsteps, changes in tone, the sound of a door closing too hard. At work, she can still perform, but she is working through a fog. Animating requires patience and precision, and she has always taken pride in it, but now she struggles to concentrate for long stretches. She stares at frames without absorbing them, rereads notes, and loses time. Her colleagues notice she is quieter. She says she is tired.

After one particularly violent incident, she leaves. The decision feels less like empowerment than survival. Even then, leaving does not bring relief right away. Instead, fear follows her into the new space of single life. She checks locks repeatedly, keeps lights on, and startles when someone walks too close behind her. She does not like sitting with her back to a door. She changes routes home. She avoids places that remind her of him, but reminders appear everywhere: a voice with a similar tone, a hand lifted in an argument on the street, the smell of the detergent he used, a particular song playing in a store. When reminders hit, her body reacts before she can think. Her heart races, her chest tightens, and for a moment she is back in the apartment, bracing for impact.

Sleep becomes broken and shallow. She falls asleep exhausted, then wakes suddenly, sometimes from dreams in which she is trapped and cannot make herself heard. Mornings begin with dread. She often lies in bed, mentally rehearsing the day as if preparation can prevent harm. She feels detached from her own life, as though she is watching herself from a distance. At times she is ashamed of how long she stayed, ashamed that she misses pieces of the relationship, ashamed that she still feels drawn to the version of him that was kind at the beginning. That confusion is painful to her; it makes her question her own judgment.

She still works as an animator, but her art has changed. She notices that the characters she draws now carry tension in their shoulders, watchful eyes, and guarded expressions. She does not always mean for them to look that way. Concentration is uneven, and some days she loses hours to spiraling thoughts about what could have happened if she had left earlier, if she had said the right thing, if she had been stronger. She is single now, and part of her feels safer for it, but another part feels isolated and uncertain about trust. She wants connection and also recoils from it. In sessions, she speaks in a steady voice, but there are moments when her hands clench in her lap and she goes quiet, as though she has just stepped back into a memory she would rather not enter.
